entries.title: Notable V8 changes from Node.js 26 to 27 (Alpha)
entries.content:
Joyee Cheung

The Node.js 27 Alpha release upgrades V8 to version 15.6, from the 14.6 used by Node.js 26, bringing several new JavaScript language features and improvements. In this post, let's explore the notable V8 changes introduced in this release that are interesting for Node.js developers.

Before we dive in, keep in mind that after Node.js switches to a new release schedule with an Alpha phase, Node.js may introduce breaking V8 changes, such as a bulk V8 upgrade, during the Alpha and Current phases. Breakages that affect the native addon ABI will come with a 

NODE_MODULE_VERSION
bump, allowing toolchains that select prebuilt native addons by ABI version to continue working. Once the 27 release enters LTS, the V8 version in this release line is expected to remain stable, and no ABI or API breaking changes are expected except in exceptional circumstances, such as critical security fixes.

JavaScript language features

New language features available by default

Math.sumPrecise(iterable)

Compared to summing up numbers in a loop, 

Math.sumPrecise
reduces the accumulation of floating-point errors.

[0.1, 0.2, 0.3].((, ) =>  + ); // 0.6000000000000001
.sumPrecise([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]); // 0.6

Intl.Locale.prototype.variants

The new 

Intl.Locale.prototype.variants
getter provides access to the variants of a locale.

new Intl.('sl-rozaj-biske').variants; // 'biske-rozaj'

Iterator methods

Several new iterator methods have been added in this release:

  • Iterator.prototype.join(separator)
  • Iterator.prototype.includes(value)
  • Iterator.zip(iterables, options)
  • Iterator.zipKeyed(obj, options)
[1, 2, 3]
  .()
  .( =>  * 2)
  .join('-'); // '2-4-6'
new (['a', 'b']).().includes('b'); // true
.zip([
  [1, 2],
  ['a', 'b'],
]).toArray(); // [[1, 'a'], [2, 'b']]
.zipKeyed({ : [1, 2], : ['a', 'b'] }).toArray();
// [{ id: 1, name: 'a' }, { id: 2, name: 'b' }]

Experimental language features behind a flag

  • --js-import-bytes
    : implements 
    import ... with { type: "bytes" }
    . Support in Node.js is not yet implemented. The related 
    import ... with { type: "text" }
     is enabled by default in V8, and supported in Node.js behind 
    --experimental-import-text
    .
  • --js-regexp-buffer-boundaries
    : implements Regular Expression Buffer Boundaries.

Some fixes have been made to these experimental language features that were already available in v26:

  • --js-defer-import-eval
    : implements 
    import defer
    . The static version already works in Node.js, while support for dynamic 
    import.defer()
    is being implemented in node#66727.
  • --js-immutable-arraybuffer
    : implements Immutable ArrayBuffer.

Changes to Math

The new version of Node.js uses LLVM's libm for some 

Math
methods, which leads to slightly different results for some inputs compared to the previous implementation. Code that compares floating point results to hard-coded values from an older version of Node.js may be broken by a difference in the last bit.
.(18);
// v26: -0.7509872467716762
// v27: -0.750987246771676
.(3);
// v26: 1.0986122886681096
// v27: 1.0986122886681098

Math.random()
now runs the xorshift128+ generator directly and no longer uses a cache, and the sequence of values returned now changes for a given 
--random-seed
.
// node --random-seed=42
.();
// v26: 0.6159659788862542
// v27: 0.22876995452731475

Changes to Date

The value returned by 

Date.prototype.getTimezoneOffset()
is no longer truncated to whole minutes. For historical dates when the time zone used a local mean time offset that is not a whole number of minutes (typically before the zone adopted standard time), the returned value can contain a fraction.
// TZ=America/Los_Angeles node
const  = new (.(1675, 0, 1));
.();
// v26: 472
// v27: 472.96666666666664
const  = new (.() + .() * 60000);
.();
// v26: '12/31/1674, 11:59:02 PM'
// v27: '1/1/1675, 12:00:00 AM'

New sorting algorithm for arrays

V8 now uses PowerSort instead of TimSort in 

Array.prototype.sort()
for bigger arrays. The sort is still stable and the result from using a consistent comparator remains the same, but tests that record comparator calls or comparators with side effects can now behave differently.
const  = .({ : 2000 }, (, ) => ( * 7919) % 1009);
let  = 0;
.((, ) => {
  ++;
  return  - ;
});
;
// v26: 19220
// v27: 19249

Changes to 
error.stack
access

The 

error.stack
getter no longer looks up the captured stack trace from the prototype chain, as required by the error stack accessor proposal. Errors created with 

new
, error subclasses and objects passed to 
Error.captureStackTrace
are not affected.
const  = new ('boom');
typeof .().stack; // No longer looks up the prototype chain
// v26: 'string'
// v27: 'undefined'

Changes to Promises and async/await

When an ES module with top-level 

await
is evaluated, as the specification requires, V8 no longer calls 

Promise.prototype.then()
in a way that looks up 
constructor
and 
Symbol.species
on the promise.

When the callback passed to 

Promise.try
returns a promise whose 

constructor
is 
Promise
in the same realm, 
Promise.try
now returns that promise directly, see ecma262#3883.
const  = .(1);
.(() => ) === ;
// v26: false
// v27: true

Changes to Atomics

Calling 

Atomics.wait()
on a worker thread that is already blocked by 
Atomics.wait()
now throws a 
TypeError
instead of crashing the process. This usually only happens when a debugger evaluates code on a worker thread blocked by 
Atomics.wait()
.

Atomics.notify()
, 
Atomics.wait()
and 
Atomics.waitAsync()
now read the length of the typed array before coercing the index, as the specification requires. If the coercion leads to a growth of the buffer, an index that is originally out of bounds still results in 
RangeError
.
const  = new (0, { : 4 });
const  = new ();
.(, {
  () {
    .(4);
    return 0;
  },
});
// v26: 0
// v27: RangeError: Invalid atomic access index

Changes to Iterator helpers

Passing a finite limit above 

2^53-1
to 
take()
 and 
drop()
leads to 
RangeError
and closes the iterator, as specified in ecma262#3776. An 
Infinity
limit is still valid.
[1, 2]
  .()
  .(2 ** 53)
  .();
// v26: [1, 2]
// v27: RangeError: 9007199254740992 must be positive

AsyncIterator.prototype[Symbol.asyncDispose]
now calls 
return()
with no arguments, as the explicit resource management proposal specifies.
const  = {
  () {
    return .({ : true });
  },
  (...) {
    .(`return() is called with ${.} argument(s)`);
    return .({ : true });
  },
};
const  = .(
  .(.((async function* () {})()))
);
await [.].call();
// v26: return() is called with 1 argument(s)
// v27: return() is called with 0 argument(s)

Changes to Modules

new import(...).x
now correctly leads to 
SyntaxError
, like 
new import(...)
:
new ('new import("x").x');
// v26: parses
// v27: SyntaxError: Cannot use new with import

A few edge cases (1, 2) that used to result in crashes during module loading now reject with appropriate errors instead.

Changes to Regular expressions

Negative lookahead and lookbehind assertions no longer match inside surrogate pairs in 

/u
and 
/v
mode.

[...'😀😀'.(/(?!.)/gv)].( => .);
// v26: [1, 3, 4]
// v27: [4]
[...'😀😀'.(/(? .);
// v26: [0, 3]
// v27: [0]

Changes to Typed arrays

TypedArray.prototype.subarray()
, when called on a length-tracking typed array subclass over a resizable ArrayBuffer without an 

end
argument, now only passes the buffer and the byte offset to the subclass constructor, and omits the third 
undefined
length argument, as the specification requires.
const  = [];
class  extends  {
  constructor(...) {
    .(.);
    super(...);
  }
}
const  = new (4, { : 8 });
new ().(1);
[1]; // arguments passed to the constructor of the subarray
// v26: 3
// v27: 2

Float16Array.prototype.indexOf()
, 
lastIndexOf()
and 
includes()
now support negative values.
const  = new ([-1.5, 2]);
.(-1.5);
// v26: false
// v27: true

TypedArray.prototype.set()
with a negative offset on an immutable buffer now throws 
TypeError
before 
RangeError
.
// node --js-immutable-arraybuffer
const  = new (new (4).transferToImmutable());
.([1], -1);
// v26: RangeError: offset is out of bounds
// v27: TypeError: Cannot perform %TypedArray%.prototype.set on a detached or out-of-bounds or immutable ArrayBuffer

Changes to Syntax and semantics

await
and 
return
inside static class initialization blocks after instance members now correctly lead to 
SyntaxError
.
// SyntaxError in both versions
class A { static { return; } }
class B { x = 1; static { return; } }
// v26: parses
// v27: SyntaxError

using
in a C-style 
for
loop initializer is now disposed once and treated as immutable, according to the explicit resource management proposal.
let  = 0;
let  = 0;
for (
  using  = {
    [.]() {
      ++;
    },
  };
   < 3;
  ++
) {}
;
// v26: 5
// v27: 1

Escaped 

get
and 
set
as class field names followed by a newline now get automatic semicolon insertion. See also test262#5134.
class C {
  g\u0065t
  a = 1;
}
Object.keys(new C());
// v26: SyntaxError: Keyword must not contain escaped characters
// v27: ['get', 'a']

delete super[key]
now checks the 
this
binding before evaluating 
key
.
class  extends  {
  constructor() {
    delete super[(.('key evaluated'), 'k')]; // before super()
    super();
  }
}
new ();
// v26: prints "key evaluated", then throws ReferenceError
// v27: throws ReferenceError without evaluating the key

new Function(...)
now consults the code generation policy before converting arguments.
// node --disallow-code-generation-from-strings
const  = {
  () {
    .('toString called');
    return 'x';
  },
};
new (, 'return x');
// v26: prints "toString called", then throws EvalError
// v27: throws EvalError without calling toString

Fatal error handling

In Node.js 27, more fatal V8 errors are now handled by Node.js's fatal error handling before aborting, so 

--report-on-fatalerror
can produce a diagnostic report in cases where Node.js would previously abort without one.

Some extreme use of language features such as overly long template literals, classes with too many elements, 

Object.defineProperties
with too many properties, a regexp that is too large to compile etc. now throw 

RangeError
instead of crashing the process. This is not guaranteed and should not be relied upon for program logic, however.

V8 serialization changes

v8.serialize()
, 
structuredClone()
 and 

postMessage
now use a new serialization format. Older Node.js releases cannot deserialize data serialized by this version and will fail with an "invalid or unsupported version" error. This version can still deserialize data serialized by older releases. The new format supports typed arrays and resizable ArrayBuffers larger than 4 GB in 
structuredClone()
and 
postMessage()
. 
v8.serialize()
currently still retains the 4 GB limit.

The 

v8.cachedDataVersionTag()
now changes whenever Node.js applies its own patches on top of V8, not only when the V8 version changes. In addition, the built-in module compilation cache and cached data from 
vm.Script
/
vm.Module
can be invalidated more often across Node.js releases. This improves safety, since a patched V8 can produce different compiled code, but it does introduce more cache misses across Node.js patch and minor releases.

V8-related memory changes

  • The default old-generation size limit is now larger on machines with 4 GB-15 GB of RAM. When the heap size limit is not specified, the default maximum old-generation size is half of physical memory/cgroup memory limit clamped between 256 MB and 4 GB. Previously this was half of physical memory capped at 2 GB, or if the machine has at least 15 GB of RAM it's capped at 4 GB. On an 8 GB machine, the default old-generation limit is now 4 GB instead of 2 GB, and on a 6 GB machine it's now 3 GB instead of 2 GB. Applications that relied on the old default to restrict the amount of memory used should set 
    --max-old-space-size
    explicitly.
  • Memory held by Buffers and ArrayBuffers is now counted in V8's global allocation limit. This changes when garbage collection gets scheduled for applications that allocate a lot of buffers outside the JavaScript heap.
  • Unused bytecode is now flushed based on time instead of garbage collection count. The bytecode of a function used to be dropped after it had not run for several major garbage collections. It can now be dropped during major garbage collection after it has not run for about 3 minutes, and is recompiled on the next call. This can change the memory usage pattern of applications with a lot of rarely used code.
  • Each native object now uses more memory: each JavaScript object that wraps a native resource, such as a socket, file handle, stream, hash or blob, may use about 16 bytes more on the JavaScript heap and about 50 bytes more outside the heap.
  • Each isolate now uses more memory for property lookup caches. In the official Node.js release, each isolate uses about 180 KB more memory. This increases the memory footprint for applications that create many worker threads.
  • The garbage collection pauses are now shorter in some worst cases, reduced from ~45 ms to ~10 ms in V8's benchmarks.
  • Creating an 
    Error
    can now use less memory because the stack frame details are only computed when 
    error.stack
    is read    .
  • There can now be fewer full garbage collections at startup. The default initial old-generation allocation limit is now 32 MB, which may delay the first full GC, depending on the workload and memory pressure.

V8 performance changes

The performance impact described here can vary depending on platform, workload and build configurations. The numbers referenced below are only relevant to the benchmarks mentioned.

Array

  • Array.prototype.flat()
    is faster on large arrays.
  • Array.prototype.copyWithin()
    is faster.
  • Array.prototype.fill()
    is faster on integers and floating point numbers.
  • Array.prototype.join()
    is faster on arrays of primitives, ~5% faster on unipoker from JetStream3.
  • Array.prototype.lastIndexOf()
    is faster on arrays of floating point numbers.
  • Array.prototype.indexOf()
    is faster on sparse arrays.
  • Array.prototype.sort()
    now uses PowerSort which performs better on adversarial inputs. Sorting small arrays with a comparator is also now faster.

Strings

  • String.prototype.split()
    is faster when the input does not contain the separator.
  • String.prototype.localeCompare()
    is faster on ASCII strings, or when the default locale is less common.

Object property access

  • Reading properties from objects with many properties or deleted properties is ~10% faster on richards and ~20% faster on espree-wtb from JetStream3.
  • Code that reads the same property from different object shapes with the same layout, e.g. instances of different classes with the same fields, remains fast for longer before falling back to the slower lookup.
  • A regression that made objects created for mocking libraries slower to write has been fixed.
  • Rest destructuring without excluded properties, e.g. 
    const { ...rest } = obj
    , is now faster.

Async/promises

  • Awaiting a promise that is already fulfilled is faster and allocates less.
  • Async generators are +6% faster for async-fs on JetStream3.
  • Async functions that call themselves recursively get optimized sooner.

RegExp

  • Regexps are compiled to machine code when used for the first time instead of after a warmup. Regexps that are run many times can be faster in execution, but regexps that are created and run only once may be slower due to the compilation cost.
  • V8 no longer turns off regexp optimization after enough regexps had been compiled.
  • Splits on the same string by the same regexp can now be cached.
  • Regexp literals are no longer re-validated when a function is compiled lazily, +6% for prismjs-startup-es6 on JetStream3.

JSON

  • JSON.parse
    is now faster on certain inputs, for example inputs that contain a lot of strings and on arrays of objects that share the same shape.

Math and BigInt

  • Due to the use of LLVM's libm, some 
    Math
    functions may have different performance characteristics compared to previous versions. The impact varies depending on the platform and the specific function.
  • Math.random()
    is now better optimized.
  • Repeated modulo division of BigInt by the same divisor is 25% faster on bigint-noble-ed25519 from JetStream3, and even faster for the primes used by most elliptic curves. This may be interesting for pure JavaScript cryptography libraries based on BigInt.

Modules and scripts

  • Source text scanning has been optimized to be ~3.5% faster in code-load from Octane.
  • Resolution of names in ESMs with many imports and exports, e.g. bundled ESM chunks is now faster.

Maglev

  • Many improvements have been made to V8's Maglev optimizing compiler, resulting in better performance for various JavaScript patterns e.g. +6% for air on JetStream3, +5% for lazy-collections on JetStream3.
  • Iteration over 
    Map
    and 
    Set
    can now be faster.
  • More 
    DataView
    accessors can now be inlined.

V8 diagnostics and tooling changes

Heap snapshots

Heap snapshots now include more detailed information about the JavaScript heap. Taking a snapshot can take about twice as long and the file is about twice as large.

  • Heap snapshots now include internal objects and numeric values. The 
    exposeInternals
    and 
    exposeNumericValues
    options of 
    v8.writeHeapSnapshot()
    and 
    v8.getHeapSnapshot()
    are ignored and considered always true. This may also increase the size of the snapshots taken.
  • Heap snapshots now contain the full source of scripts in the application instead of truncating them to the first 1024 characters. The heap snapshots now also include additional 
    scopes
    , 
    scope_context_vars
    and 
    scope_uses
    sections     that describe the variables in the scopes. Newer versions of DevTools use this data to find unused captured variables. This can expose more application code and secrets embedded in source, and as usual, heap snapshots should be treated as sensitive data.
  • The global object and the global proxy are now named 
    global [JSGlobalObject]
    and 
    global [JSGlobalProxy]
    instead of 
    global (global)
    and 
    global (global*)
    . Tools that parse the older names from the heap snapshots should be updated.

CPU and heap profiles

  • Function names and URLs are now escaped correctly in profiles serialized as JSON.
  • Optimized functions that inline code from other scripts no longer corrupt the jitdump file written with --perf-prof, so now frames from these functions can be showed correctly by 
    perf inject
    .
  • Sampling heap profile retrieval can be faster by about 30% in local benchmarks due to more efficient use of strings.

Inspector and debugging

  • Debugger.setInstrumentationBreakpoint
    now works for Node.js CommonJS modules.
  • Support for live editing via the inspector has been fully removed. 
    Debugger.setScriptSource
     now always fails with "setScriptSource functionality no longer available". This feature was previously deprecated and put behind the 
    --inspector-live-edit
    flag, it has now been completely removed.
  • New protocol capabilities: 
    • Debugger.evaluateOnCallFrame
      accepts a 
      scopeNumber
       to evaluate in an outer scope.
    • Scopes now report an experimental 
      empty
      flag      .
  • Several crashes (1, 2, 3) that could occur while using the debugger have been fixed.

Tracing

  • In the 27.0.0 alpha build, most V8 trace events now no longer appear in the files written by 
    --trace-event-categories
    due to V8's migration to Perfetto-style macros. Support for building with Perfetto by default is in progress. 
    --trace-gc
    and the 
    gc
    entries of 
    perf_hooks
    are not affected. Downstream distributors who build with Perfetto can configure Node.js with 
    --shared-perfetto
    to link to a shared Perfetto SDK.
  • The 
    disabled-by-default-v8.gc
    trace category now produces fewer events. The more frequent per-step garbage collection events have been moved to the 
    disabled-by-default-v8.gc_extra
    category    .

WebAssembly changes

WebAssembly removals and deprecations

  • asm.js is no longer compiled to WebAssembly. This means asm.js modules can still run as ordinary JavaScript, but code that depended on asm.js optimizations may be slower, and users will no longer see the "Converted asm.js to WebAssembly" messages.
  • WebAssembly.Function
    behind 
    --experimental-wasm-type-reflection
    from the type reflection proposal was removed.

WebAssembly flag changes

  • --experimental-wasm-
    flags are now renamed 
    --wasm-
    . The old names are no longer accepted.
  • --wasm-lazy-validation
    was removed. Invalid functions are now always reported when a module is compiled and this can no longer be disabled.
  • --wasm-async-compilation
    was removed, which means there's no longer a 
    --no-wasm-async-compilation
    that makes the asynchronous compilation API synchronous.
  • --experimental-wasm-exnref
    , 
    --experimental-wasm-branch-hinting
     and 
    --experimental-wasm-rab-integration
     have been removed, as the features they enabled are now always on.

WebAssembly optimizations

  • The 
    memory.copy
    and 
    memory.fill
    instructions, which are typically used in compiled code for 
    memcpy
    and 
    memset
    , are now inlined in optimized code instead of calling into the runtime, resulting in a ~12% speedup on a bulk memory benchmark.
  • Calling exported functions that take or return structs, arrays and other reference types is about twice as fast on a microbenchmark.
  • new WebAssembly.Table({ element, initial }, value)
    now fills the table faster, and an invalid 
    value
    now throws before the table is allocated.
  • On arm64, more optimizations for Wasm SIMD code are now enabled by default. They were previously behind 
    --wasm-simd-opt
    . On x64 these optimizations are not available.

Removed and renamed V8 flags

Renamed

OldNew
--experimental-wasm-
--wasm-
--experimental-wasm-simd-opt
(arm64 only)
--future-wasm-simd-opt
--abort-on-contradictory-flags
--flag-processing-mode=abort-on-error
--exit-on-contradictory-flags
--flag-processing-mode=exit-on-error
--allow-overwriting-for-next-flag
--flag-processing-mode=ignore-contradictions

Removed

  • --js-upsert
  • --js-regexp-escape
  • --js-promise-try
  • --js-error-iserror
  • --js-base-64
  • --js-explicit-resource-management
  • --js-sum-precise
  • --js-intl-locale-variants
  • --js-atomics-pause
  • --js-regexp-duplicate-named-groups
  • --js-regexp-modifiers
  • --bytecode-old-age
  • --flush-code-based-on-time
  • --detailed-error-stack-trace
  • --heap-profiler-show-hidden-objects
  • --expose-ignition-statistics
  • --riscv-c-extension
    (RISC-V only)
  • --turbo-compress-frame-translations
  • --inspector-live-edit
  • --max-fast-properties
  • --validate-asm
  • --wasm-lazy-validation
  • --wasm-async-compilation

entries.title: Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Security Releases
entries.content:
OpenJS Ecosystem Sustainability Program partners

Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Security Releases

The Node.js Project

Summary

The Node.js project will release new versions of the 26.x, 24.x, 22.x releases lines on or shortly after, Wednesday, November 11, 2026 in order to address:

The highest severity issue fixed in this release is HIGH.

Impact

The highest severity issue fixed in the 26.x release line is HIGH. The highest severity issue fixed in the 24.x release line is HIGH. The highest severity issue fixed in the 22.x release line is HIGH.

It's important to note that End-of-Life versions are always affected when a security release occurs. To ensure your system's security, please use an up-to-date version as outlined in our Release Schedule.

Release timing

Releases will be available on, or shortly after, Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

Contact and future updates

The current Node.js security policy can be found at https://nodejs.org/en/security/. Please follow the process outlined in https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/master/SECURITY.md if you wish to report a vulnerability in Node.js.

Subscribe to the low-volume announcement-only nodejs-sec mailing list at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/nodejs-sec to stay up to date on security vulnerabilities and security-related releases of Node.js and the projects maintained in the nodejs GitHub organization.
